title: Declared types and var (type inference)
hook: Every variable in C# has a type the compiler knows before your program runs. The `var` keyword asks the compiler to figure out that type from the value you assign — it is not JavaScript `var` and not a free pass like TypeScript `any`.

blocks.text: A **type** tells the compiler what kind of data a variable holds — a whole number (`int`), text (`string`), true/false (`bool`), and so on. You can write the type yourself (`int count = 10`) or let the compiler infer it with `var` (`var count = 10`). After either spelling, `count` is an `int` for the rest of its life. C# is **statically typed**: the type is fixed at compile time and checked on every use.

entries.plainDefinition: The type the compiler assigns to a variable. It never changes after declaration and is enforced on every operation.
entries.example: Once `var x = 10` makes `x` an `int`, you cannot assign `"hello"` to `x`.

entries.plainDefinition: A C# keyword that tells the compiler to infer the variable's type from the initializer on the right-hand side.
entries.example: `var name = "Ada";` is exactly the same as `string name = "Ada";` after compilation.

entries.plainDefinition: The value (or expression) you assign when declaring a variable. `var` requires one — you cannot write `var x;` alone.
entries.example: `var total = 1 + 2;` — the compiler sees `3` and picks `int`.

blocks.text: Types catch mistakes before you ship. If you try `int count = 10; count = "ten";`, the build fails immediately — no silent corruption at run time. In a worker that reads an Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) message, knowing `attemptCount` is an `int` (not a loose string) prevents bad math and bad retries. `var` is a readability tool: when the right-hand side already makes the type obvious (`new List<string>()`), spelling `var` avoids repeating yourself without losing safety.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: `var` is compile-time type inference. The Intermediate Language (IL) output is identical to writing the type name. It is unrelated to JavaScript `var` hoisting and unrelated to the `dynamic` keyword.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: From source code to a fixed type

items.title: You write a declaration
items.body: Either `int score = 95` or `var score = 95`. Both forms include an initializer.

items.title: The compiler infers or reads the type
items.body: For `var`, the compiler looks at the right-hand side. `95` is an `int` literal, so the variable becomes `int`. Target-typed `new` also works: `List<string> names = new()` — the empty `new()` picks up `List<string>` from the left side.

items.title: The type is locked in
items.body: From this point, every assignment must match. The compiler rejects `score = "A"` with a clear error.

items.title: IL stores the real type
items.body: Whether you wrote `var` or `int`, the compiled assembly metadata says `Int32`. There is no run-time type lookup for `var`.

diagram.title: How var resolves a type
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A["var count = 10"] --> B[Roslyn compiler]
  B --> C["Inferred type: int"]
  C --> D["IL metadata: Int32"]
  D --> E[CLR runs with fixed type]

snippet.label: var is inference, not dynamic
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `999` is an `int` literal, so `attemptCap` is `int`. Line 4: `new List<decimal>()` makes the type obvious — `var` saves typing `List<decimal>` twice. Line 7: `var` always needs a value on the right; `var pending;` does not compile.

snippet.label: Target-typed new with explicit left side
snippet.explanation: Line 1: C# 9+ lets `new()` copy the type from the left (`Dictionary<string,int>`). Line 4: `var` infers `Dictionary<string,string>` from the constructor. Line 7: the compiler still knows key and value types — wrong key type is caught at build time.

snippet.label: When var picks a too-general type
snippet.explanation: Line 4: `var` infers from the expression's compile-time type. Because `payload` is declared `object`, `data` is also `object` — you lose access to `Body` without a cast. Line 7: cast first (or assign to a typed variable) so the compiler knows the real shape.

blocks.title: var in three languages
rows: Infers a static type from initializer
Infers a type, erased at run time
No at compile time; yes at run time

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Equating C# `var` with JavaScript `var` (scope and hoisting) or with `dynamic` (run-time binding). Using `var` when the right-hand side is `object` and you needed a specific Data Transfer Object (DTO) — inference will pick `object`. Thinking `var` is slower: it is purely a compile-time shortcut with zero run-time cost.

interviewTakeaways: `var` is compile-time inference; IL is identical to writing the type name.
You cannot change a variable's type after declaration.
Parameters, fields without initializers, and `var` without a right-hand side are not inference sites.
commonPitfalls: Equating C# `var` with JS `var` (scope/hoisting) or with `dynamic`.
Using `var` when the right-hand side is a factory that returns `object` and you needed a more specific type.
Thinking `var` is slower — it is not a run-time lookup.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `var` is a binding with function scope and no static type. C# `var` is only a spelling for an inferred static type that never changes.
TypeScript `let n = 1` infers `number` similarly, but TypeScript types erase at run time. C# inferred types remain in assembly metadata the Common Language Runtime (CLR) can read.
